narration: Have you ever been asked to do something that felt a little scary — and said yes anyway? Maybe it was speaking in front of people. Maybe it was trying something you'd never done before. Maybe it was just walking into a room full of strangers.
visual_description: Youth-friendly illustration of a young person facing a new, slightly nerve-wracking situation
on_screen_text: What happens when we step outside what's easy?

narration: That feeling — that mix of nervous and excited — has a name. Over the next few minutes, you're going to learn what it's called, why it matters, and why the program you're starting today is built entirely around it. Welcome. You're about to begin something called ACT.
Let's start the way this program is meant to start. {{arabic:basmala}}. Thank you for being here.

I want you to know something right away: this program is not going to feel like a classroom. It's casual. It's informal. You're allowed to be yourself in it. What you're starting is a series of exercises, activities, and games — and I want you to bring real enthusiasm and initiative to all of it, because what you put in is what you'll get out.

This program is called ACT — which stands for Attitude Cultivates Transformation. That's exactly what it is: a program built on the idea that your attitude — how you choose to face things — is what actually transforms you.

ACT is an interactive program designed to equip you with real skills for your future — the kind of skills the job market actually asks for, and the kind that help you build your career — through social and voluntary work. It wasn't built generically. It was designed specifically with you in mind, and you've been chosen to be part of it, alongside other young people who share the same bright future ahead of them.

Before we go further, it's worth knowing who's behind this. ACT is a global initiative by the NAMA Foundation. Working alongside them is Ghadan — a not-for-profit consultancy and capacity-building foundation. Take a second and think about that phrase, "not-for-profit." It means an organization that doesn't take any profit for its partners or stakeholders — everything it does is aimed at its mission, which here is increasing social participation in your community.
visual_description: Organization logos: NAMA Foundation, Ghadan (Consulting & Capacity Building), NICE (Nama Integrated Centre for Excellence)

narration: There's also something ahead of you to look forward to: an awards ceremony, held across Tanzania, where the strongest groups will be celebrated — with official guests in attendance. So everything you do in this program can lead somewhere real.
visual_description: Celebratory, hopeful illustration hinting at a future awards ceremony

narration: Here's the shape of the whole journey you're starting. ACT is built from four units, and each one answers a different question and builds different skills.

Unit 1 is Self-Awareness. This is where you are right now. In this unit, you'll get to know yourself — your identity, your strengths, your capabilities — through games and activities that are actually engaging, not just informative.
visual_description: Unit 1 section-divider graphic from the curriculum slides

narration: Unit 2 is Social Awareness. Here, you'll become aware of your society — its strengths and its limits — and understand what it really means to be part of a collective community. You'll watch examples from other societies too, and keep learning through games.
visual_description: Unit 2 section-divider graphic from the curriculum slides
on_screen_text: Unit 2: Social Awareness — Who are others?

narration: Unit 3 is Awareness of Social Issues. In this unit, you'll become aware of the social issues that actually exist around you, understand how serious they are, and start thinking about how to contribute to solving them. You'll build a sense of social justice, and by the end, you'll choose a social issue you personally want to work on.
visual_description: Unit 3 section-divider graphic from the curriculum slides
on_screen_text: Unit 3: Social Issues — What do others suffer from?

narration: Unit 4 is Social Initiatives. This is the biggest unit — it covers half of the whole program, and it's often the most fun and rewarding part. Here you'll learn the real fundamentals of planning and managing a project. You'll choose your own project, build it, and share what you achieved with the people around you.
visual_description: Unit 4 section-divider graphic from the curriculum slides
on_screen_text: Unit 4: Social Initiatives — What can I offer?

narration: Notice the shape of that journey: who am I, who are others, what do others struggle with, and what can I actually offer? That's the path ACT is going to walk you through, one unit at a time.
on_screen_text: Who am I? → Who are others? → What do they suffer from? → What can I offer?

narration: Before we go any further, let me tell you something about the person guiding you through this program — and I want you to test yourself a little. I'm going to tell you three things about myself. Two are true. One is not. See if you can guess which one.

Here's something trainers in this program love to do on day one: they share two true things about themselves, and one lie — and let the room guess which is which. It's a simple trick, but it works, because it turns being taught at into getting to know someone. So here's a challenge for you: think of two true things about yourself, and one believable lie. Keep them in your head, or better, write them down. You'll get a chance to try this out on someone in your life today. That's the spirit this whole program runs on. So — how excited are you to get started?

Let's begin the way this program always begins: by breaking the ice. Grab a piece of paper — or your workbook if you have one — and tear or cut it into three small pieces. On each piece, write one thing about yourself: a hobby, a skill, or a personal trait. Just one per piece. Take your time with this — it doesn't have to be impressive, it just has to be true.

Now it's your turn. Pause the video here. Write your three things — one hobby, one skill, one trait. When you're done, come back and press play. If you're watching together with a group: once everyone has their three papers, fold them, mix them together, and have each person draw three at random, then go find who wrote each one. If you're watching alone, keep your three papers somewhere you'll see them again — you'll be building on this idea of "who am I" throughout the program.

That's a small moment, but it matters more than it seems. You just put into words three real, specific things about who you are. Hold onto that. Self-awareness — which is exactly what Unit 1 is about — starts with small, honest moments like this one.

Now that we've broken the ice, let's talk about something important: the kind of space we want this to be. Think about it for a second — what would you want from the people around you, and from me, to make this program feel smooth and worthwhile? What would help you feel comfortable enough to actually speak your mind here?
on_screen_text: What makes a space feel safe?

narration: Here are a few examples of the kinds of things that usually come up: putting phones away except for real emergencies, showing up on time, and — maybe most importantly — nobody making fun of anyone else's ideas or contributions. Think about it this way: what do you think about people interrupting each other while they're talking? Should we agree not to do that? And what about people who laugh at someone else's opinion while they're sharing it?
visual_description: Idea/lightbulb icon from the curriculum slides
on_screen_text: Phones down · Be on time · No mocking ideas

narration: If you're watching this in a group: talk through these questions together, agree on your own list of ground rules, write them down somewhere everyone can see, and have everyone sign it. If you're watching alone: pause here and write down, in your own words, the two or three things you personally commit to.
Here's the important part: this isn't a list of rules being handed down to you. You are the ones deciding how this program runs. That's what makes it a safe space — you have real control over it.

One more thing before we move on: a short survey. There are no grades on this — it's simply a way to capture where your knowledge stands right now, so that by the end of this journey, you can look back and see how far you've come.

Now it's your turn. Pause the video, and rate yourself honestly, right now: I understand what ACT is and what it's for. I could name at least one of the four units. I know what the 'challenge zone' means. I feel confident stepping outside my comfort zone. I'm excited to start this program. Answer honestly, keep your answers somewhere safe, and press play when you're done. We'll come back to this at the very end of the program.

Alright. Now we get to the heart of this lesson — and honestly, to an idea that's going to follow you through this entire program. Picture three circles. The first is your Comfort Zone — call it "Easy." The second is your Challenge Zone — call it "Let's Go." And the third is your Pain Zone — call it "No Way!"
visual_description: Simple three-zone diagram (Comfort/Easy, Challenge/Let's Go, Pain/No Way) — no existing digital asset found; originally three physical signs taped around the training room

narration: Here's what each one actually means. The Easy zone is where you do things without needing to think hard or put in any real effort — it's automatic. The Impossible zone is where you run into something you genuinely don't know how to tackle, and it leaves you stuck. And the Let's Go zone — the challenge zone — is where you have some idea how to tackle something, but not yet enough experience to do it easily. That's exactly what makes it a challenge.
visual_description: Same three-zone diagram, now annotated with each zone's definition
on_screen_text: Easy = no effort · Let's Go = stretch · No Way = stuck

narration: I'm going to walk you through five situations. For each one, I want you to actually picture yourself in it, and decide — honestly — which zone you'd be in: Easy, Let's Go, or No Way.

First: Suppose you're on a trip with your teacher and your classmates, and suddenly the plane develops a technical problem mid-flight. The pilot tells everyone to jump out with a parachute. Which zone are you in?
Second: You have to dive into the ocean, and you're told there are sharks nearby — but the locals say these particular sharks are peaceful and won't hurt you. Which zone?
Third: You have to stand up and speak in front of 700 people. Which zone?
Fourth: You're handed a strange meal, and you have no idea what's actually in it. Which zone?
Fifth: You have to voice your honest opinion in front of important decision-makers — and you already know they disagree with you. Which zone?

Pause the video now, and for each of those five, decide which zone you landed in — and if you can, think about why. If you're watching in a group: after each scenario, have everyone move to a different part of the room representing their zone, and ask a few people to explain their choice out loud.

Let's think through what just happened. What did you actually discover about yourself in that exercise? Are the three zones clear to you now — comfort, challenge, and pain? What's the real difference between them? Now think about how each zone feels. What do you feel toward the comfort zone? Toward the challenge zone? Toward the pain zone?
on_screen_text: What did you discover? What do you feel?

narration: Here's a harder question. Why did some of those situations feel "easy" to you, and not to someone else? Why did some feel like "Let's Go," and others like "impossible"? And think back on your own life — have the times you felt genuinely challenged ever actually made you stronger? Does staying in the comfort zone ever really grow your knowledge or your power? Does the pain zone add anything to you at all? And does the challenge zone actually benefit you, strengthen you?
on_screen_text: Why does the challenge zone feel different?

narration: So here's the real question this whole exercise is pointing toward: which zone do we actually need to spend our time in, if we want to keep growing and learning? A lot of people get this wrong at first — it's easy to assume the answer is the comfort zone, because it's comfortable. But the zone that actually grows your strengths and capabilities — the zone that becomes the ladder toward becoming a capable, influential person — is the challenge zone.
on_screen_text: The challenge zone is the growth zone.

narration: God created us with the ability to develop and to advance. And the real difference between an exceptional human being and an average one isn't talent — it's how much they've actually used and benefited from that ability.
on_screen_text: The ability to grow is a gift.

narration: The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Paradise is surrounded by hardships." And hardship is about as close as it gets to the challenge zone.

Think about it — a person can grow so much. Change for the better — psychologically, spiritually, emotionally, even financially — just by taking one step: out of the comfort zone, and into the challenge zone. Youth — the stage of life you're in right now — is the very best period to learn, to face challenges, and to grow in strength, knowledge, and power, for your own future and for the future of your community.
on_screen_text: Youth is the best time to grow.

narration: This exercise, small as it seems, can genuinely change your life. And here's something worth sitting with: many of us are serving our community, in some real way, for the first time in our lives through this program. Children think enjoyment comes from taking. But people who've actually lived know that the truest pleasures in life are the moments of giving — not taking.
on_screen_text: The truest pleasure is giving, not taking.

narration: This program — ACT — is built to deliberately put you in the challenge zone, again and again, so that you walk out of it having genuinely added something new to who you are.
on_screen_text: ACT keeps you in the challenge zone — on purpose.

narration: Now let's see this in real life, not just as a theory. It's the story of the Koh Panyee Island Soccer Team, from Thailand — a group of boys who built their own soccer field out of nothing, in a place nobody expected a soccer team to come from. Pause the video now and watch the short film linked below — 'The Koh Panyee Island Soccer Team.' When it's finished, come back and press play.
visual_description: On-screen link/QR to the official source video rather than an embedded copy, to avoid unclear third-party licensing on the downloaded file found in the original PowerPoint, and to keep this lesson's own video runtime inside the 5-20 minute policy. Source reference: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jU4oA3kkAWU (verify link is still live before production).
on_screen_text: Pause here — watch the linked film, then resume

narration: Take a moment with what you just watched. What did you actually see happen in that video? How did people react when that soccer field was first built? Why do you think their reactions changed once the team actually started playing — and how did it feel watching them win?
on_screen_text: What did you see? What changed?

narration: Why do you think those boys were able to beat so many different, more established teams? And why were they able to keep playing hard, even through bad weather?
on_screen_text: Why were they able to win?

narration: Here's the truth underneath that story: if it hadn't been for the harsh, uneven ground they had to play on — and the pain they had to push through — they would never have developed the skill it took to beat those other teams under normal conditions. Hardship and challenge are what build strong people. Whenever you're in the middle of a genuinely tough situation, that's not a sign something's gone wrong. It's a sign you're growing.

That same team went on to win seven championships in a row. Facing a challenge can be hard at the beginning, and yes, you might even be mocked for it, the way those boys were mocked for trying to play soccer on a wooden field on an island. But the same people who mocked them became their biggest supporters, the moment they saw how skilled they'd become, and how much they believed in themselves.

If you want to be a leader in your community, hold onto that competitive mindset. Whenever a challenge comes your way, ask yourself: what can I learn from this? What skill is going to come out of the other side of this? Even everyday challenges — like having to work to earn money — are quietly teaching you real, transferable skills that the job market values everywhere in the world.
on_screen_text: What can I learn from this challenge?

narration: Today, you were welcomed into ACT — a program built on the idea that your attitude is what transforms you. You learned what this program actually is, who's behind it, and the four-unit journey you're about to walk: who you are, who others are, what others struggle with, and what you can offer. You helped build the ground rules for a space where you can genuinely speak your mind. And most importantly, you were introduced to the three learning zones, and the idea that real growth only happens when you deliberately step into the challenge zone.
on_screen_text: Welcome · Program overview · Safe space · Learning zones

narration: Right now, if you can, say this to yourself — out loud if you're comfortable, or quietly if you're not: "I am a change maker. I live in the challenge zone." If you're watching in a group: gather in a circle and say this together, in unison.
on_screen_text: "I am a change maker. I live in the challenge zone."

narration: Hold onto that. Because in the next lesson, we're going to go even deeper into the first real question of this journey — the question of who you actually are. I'll see you there.
